cards.front: Any membraneless body that concentrates proteins and nucleic acids is a {{c1::biomolecular condensate}}, regardless of how it formed.
cards.quote: Any membraneless body that concentrates proteins and nucleic acids is a biomolecular condensate, whatever made it.

cards.front: In liquid-liquid phase separation, a solution demixes into a dense phase and a {{c1::dilute phase}}.
cards.back: The nuclear dilute phase is the nucleoplasm around the droplets.
cards.quote: above a certain concentration a solution demixes into a dense phase (the droplets) and a dilute phase

cards.front: How is multivalency thought to promote protein phase separation?
cards.back: Many weak, reversible binding sites per molecule allow repeated interactions among molecules.
cards.quote: many weak, reversible binding sites per molecule (repeated domains, disordered regions, RNA; that lesson).

cards.front: What can a bright nuclear spot establish about its contents, and what can it not establish?
cards.back: It establishes that something is concentrated, but not the mechanism that concentrated it.
cards.quote: A bright spot shows that something is concentrated, not how.

cards.front: At equilibrium under fixed conditions, more of a protein is added above its saturation concentration. If that protein demixes on its own, what happens?
cards.back: Dense-phase volume increases, while protein concentrations inside and outside the bodies remain fixed.
cards.quote: the extra adds dense-phase volume (bigger drops or more of them) while the inside and outside concentrations stay fixed.

cards.front: More protein is added to a fixed set of binding sites that cannot grow. Where does the extra protein go?
cards.back: Site occupancy rises, so spots brighten until the sites fill; after saturation, the outside concentration rises.
cards.quote: the extra raises occupancy: spots brighten until the sites fill, and only then does the outside climb.

cards.front: Increasing a protein enlarges its nuclear bodies without changing their brightness or the outside concentration. What conclusion is justified?
cards.back: The pattern supports the simple one-protein phase model, but does not prove it; alternative mechanisms must still be tested.
cards.why: The inference rests on asking where added protein goes and treating each predicted pattern as support rather than proof.
cards.quote: Each pattern supports its model; neither proves it alone.

cards.front: Why does a round nuclear focus not establish that it is a liquid droplet?
cards.back: Sub-resolution clusters can also look round, so roundness identifies neither softness nor formation mechanism.
cards.quote: Roundness alone shows neither softness nor mechanism, because clusters below the resolution of the microscope look round too.
cards.section: Why looking harder does not help

cards.front: Two nuclear bodies approach and appear to become one. What additional observation would make fusion more convincing?
cards.back: Show that the merged body relaxes into one round body; drifting clusters can otherwise mimic fusion.
cards.quote: clusters that drift together can look merged unless that relaxation is seen.
cards.section: Why looking harder does not help

cards.front: FRAP measures molecular {{c1::turnover}}, which can result from binding and unbinding as well as from a liquid phase.
cards.back: Fluorescence recovery alone is therefore not diagnostic of a liquid droplet.
cards.quote: FRAP, fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (that lesson), measures turnover, which binding and unbinding also give.
cards.section: Why looking harder does not help

cards.front: A nuclear body dissolves after 1,6-hexanediol treatment. What must be checked before attributing dissolution to disrupted liquid interactions?
cards.back: Check the reagent's other effects, especially changes to chromatin motion that could disrupt the body by another mechanism.
cards.quote: A reagent that changes chromatin this much cannot tell you which mechanism held a body together.
cards.section: Why looking harder does not help

cards.front: In half-body FRAP, the bleached half recovers as the unbleached half dims, while adjacent nucleoplasm barely changes. What does this pattern suggest?
cards.back: Molecules mix inside the body faster than they cross its boundary, which favours a phase without proving one.
cards.quote: A droplet has a boundary, so molecules are expected to mix inside it faster than they cross its edge.
cards.section: Why looking harder does not help

cards.front: Why can even the expected half-body FRAP pattern fail to prove phase separation?
cards.back: Real condensate boundaries may only weakly slow crossing, while molecules rebinding within a dense fixed-site cluster can also mix internally.
cards.why: The same measured motion can arise from more than one mechanism.
cards.quote: molecules that rebind sites inside a dense cluster can also mix internally.
cards.section: Why looking harder does not help

cards.front: Below a one-protein phase's saturation concentration, c_sat, no bodies form and {{c1::outside concentration equals total concentration}}.
cards.back: The outside-versus-total graph follows a 45° line.
cards.quote: Below the saturation concentration, c_sat, there are no bodies and outside equals total: a 45° line.

cards.front: Why does the outside concentration for far-from-full binding sites form a straight line below the 45° line?
cards.back: Each molecule has the same binding chance, so a fixed fraction remains outside as total concentration rises.
cards.quote: each molecule has the same chance of being bound at any moment, so a fixed fraction stays outside

cards.front: For a simple phase, mass balance is {{c1::c_total = c_sat × (1 − φ) + c_dense × φ}}.
cards.back: Here φ is the fraction of nuclear volume occupied by the dense phase.
cards.quote: c_total = c_sat × (1 − φ) + c_dense × φ

cards.front: A simple one-protein phase has c_sat = 1 μM, c_dense = 50 μM, and c_total = 4 μM. What fraction of nuclear volume is dense phase?
cards.quote: φ goes from 1/49 = 2.0% of the nucleus at 2 μM, through 3/49 = 6.1% at 4 μM

cards.front: For c_sat = 1 μM and c_dense = 50 μM, c_total rises from 2 to 8 μM. By what factor does dense-phase volume rise?
cards.back: φ rises from (2−1)/49 = 1/49 to (8−1)/49 = 7/49. Dense-phase volume therefore rises sevenfold.
cards.quote: Volume tracks the excess over c_sat, which goes from 1 to 7, not the total, which goes from 2 to 8.

cards.front: As a protein's total concentration rises, its outside concentration stays near 1 μM and total body volume grows at unchanged brightness. Which model is supported?
cards.back: The simple one-protein phase model: extra protein increases dense-phase volume while dilute- and dense-phase concentrations stay nearly fixed.
cards.quote: Protein A: outside 1.0, 1.0 and 1.1 μM, while the total body volume grows at the same brightness.

cards.front: A protein's outside concentration remains about 0.7–0.75 of its total while its foci brighten in proportion. What mechanism is supported?
cards.back: Binding to fixed sites that are far from full; a constant outside fraction produces a straight line through zero.
cards.quote: A constant fraction outside is the straight line through zero: sites far from full.

cards.front: The region occupied by an interphase chromosome is its {{c1::chromosome territory}}.
cards.back: The chromosome partly unpacks after mitosis but does not spread throughout the nucleus.
cards.quote: each one fills a region of its own, a chromosome territory.

cards.front: How can chromosomes occupy distinct territories without being completely separate?
cards.back: Each keeps its own region, but loose chromatin loops intermingle where neighbouring territories meet.
cards.quote: Neighbouring territories overlapped at their edges, and how much two chromosomes overlapped correlated with how often that pair takes part in translocations

cards.front: Chromosome pairs that overlap more at territory edges also undergo translocations more often after irradiation. Does this show that overlap causes a particular translocation?
cards.back: No. The association is a correlation and does not establish that overlap caused any given translocation.
cards.quote: That is a correlation, not proof that overlap causes any given translocation.

cards.front: What does a sequenced Hi-C junction report?
cards.back: It joins two genome segments that lay close together in space when chromatin was cross-linked.
cards.quote: segments lying close in space end up in one DNA molecule, and sequencing millions of these junctions maps which parts of the genome touch.

cards.front: Hi-C compartment A is open, gene-rich, mostly active chromatin; compartment B is {{c1::closed, mostly quiet chromatin}}.
cards.back: The two chromatin types segregate into genome-wide compartments.
cards.quote: A (open, gene-rich, mostly active) and B (closed, mostly quiet).

cards.front: A population Hi-C map shows frequent contact between two regions. Can it place both regions together in every individual nucleus?
cards.back: No. Population maps report average contact frequency across millions of cells, not positions in any one nucleus.
cards.quote: they report how often two regions are near each other, not where they sit in one nucleus.

cards.front: Why is imaging thin chromosome-painted sections better than imaging a whole nucleus for detecting intermingling at territory edges?
cards.back: Thin sections remove much of the above-and-below light that blurs edges in a whole nucleus.
cards.quote: in a whole nucleus light from above and below blurs every edge.

cards.front: A {{c1::nuclear body}} is a nucleoplasmic region where particular molecules are concentrated without a surrounding membrane.
cards.quote: A nuclear body is a region of the nucleoplasm where particular molecules are concentrated, with no membrane around it.

cards.front: What is the principal function of the nucleolus?
cards.back: Ribosome biogenesis.
cards.quote: The largest, the nucleolus, carries out ribosome biogenesis.

cards.front: What does the fibrillar centre of a mammalian nucleolus contain?
cards.back: It contains rDNA and the RNA polymerase I machinery that transcribes it.
cards.quote: The fibrillar centre holds the rDNA and the machinery of RNA polymerase I, the enzyme that transcribes it.

cards.front: What occurs in the dense fibrillar component of a mammalian nucleolus?
cards.back: Newly made pre-rRNA begins to be processed there; the component is rich in fibrillarin.
cards.quote: the newly made ribosomal RNA precursor (pre-rRNA) begins to be processed.

cards.front: What occurs in the granular component of a mammalian nucleolus?
cards.back: Ribosomal subunits are assembled before export; the component is rich in NPM1.
cards.quote: The outer granular component, rich in nucleophosmin (NPM1), is where ribosomal subunits are assembled before export.

cards.front: What molecules are concentrated in nuclear speckles?
cards.back: Pre-mRNA splicing factors that exchange with the nucleoplasm.
cards.quote: Pre-mRNA splicing factors, which exchange with the nucleoplasm (splicing)

cards.front: What molecules identify Cajal bodies?
cards.back: Coilin and components of the small nuclear RNPs that splice pre-mRNA.
cards.quote: Coilin, their marker, and components of the small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs) that splice pre-mRNA

cards.front: What molecules are concentrated in PML bodies?
cards.back: The PML protein that builds them, SUMO, and partner proteins.
cards.quote: The PML protein that builds them, SUMO and partner proteins

cards.front: What forms the scaffold of a paraspeckle, and what else does it hold?
cards.back: The long noncoding RNA NEAT1 forms its scaffold and holds bound proteins.
cards.quote: Their scaffold, the long noncoding RNA NEAT1, and its bound proteins

cards.front: What observations make the Xenopus oocyte nucleolus a strong case for a liquid phase?
cards.back: Its fibrillarin-rich and NPM1-rich layers behave as coexisting, nonmixing liquids, and purified proteins plus RNA reproduce the layering.
cards.quote: the fibrillarin-rich and NPM1-rich layers behave as two liquids that coexist without mixing, and purified nucleolar proteins mixed with RNA reproduce the layering
cards.section: Real bodies: one strong case, one split verdict

cards.front: How does protein-mediated chromatin bridging differ from a liquid protein droplet?
cards.back: Bridges cross-link distant chromatin segments, collapsing the fibre into a chromatin globule rather than a liquid pool of protein.
cards.quote: the result is a globule of chromatin, not a liquid drop of the protein.
cards.section: Real bodies: one strong case, one split verdict

cards.front: HP1 foci appear liquid-like in one organism, but half-body FRAP favours collapsed chromatin globules in another. What general conclusion follows?
cards.back: The mechanism of heterochromatin organization can differ by system; neither result establishes one mechanism for all heterochromatin.
cards.why: This combines organism-specific evidence with the rule that a finding in one system need not generalize to all systems.
cards.quote: Neither study speaks for all heterochromatin.
cards.section: Real bodies: one strong case, one split verdict

cards.front: Outside concentration stays nearly flat as total protein rises, but fixed-size foci brighten and eventually stop brightening. What mechanism is favoured?
cards.back: Cooperative binding to a fixed set of sites: the sites fill over a narrow range, then outside concentration rises.
cards.quote: the sites stay nearly empty at low concentration and then fill over a narrow range, like a threshold

cards.front: Why can one component's rising dilute-phase concentration fail to rule out phase separation of a nuclear body?
cards.back: A multicomponent mixture need not buffer the concentration of every individual component.
cards.quote: a mixture of several components, which need not buffer each one.

cards.front: A nuclear body forms at a chromatin site even though average nuclear protein concentration is below the global phase-separation threshold. How could this still fit phase separation?
cards.back: Chromatin could act as a local seed, capturing protein until the local concentration crosses the threshold despite a lower global average.
cards.why: This applies the lesson's engineered-seed result to chromatin without adding another mechanism.
cards.quote: local capture of a protein on a small engineered seed triggered phase separation below the global concentration needed for it.

cards.front: A protein passes concentration and FRAP tests for phase separation. Does that establish that the resulting body is required for its cellular function?
cards.back: No. Formation mechanism and functional necessity are separate claims, so function must be tested independently from body assembly.
cards.why: Passing physical tests supports how a body forms, not whether the body is necessary for a biological outcome.
cards.quote: A protein that passes has not been shown to need the body for any function.

cards.front: Design a test of whether protein X's nuclear foci, rather than X alone, are needed for transcription.
cards.back: Tag endogenous X; vary its level and measure inside, outside, volume, and brightness; use half-body FRAP and a DNA-binding, multivalency-deficient mutant; then alter gene-focus location independently and assay transcription.
cards.why: The design separates assembly mechanism from transcriptional function and includes controls for tagging, localization, and X's nonassembly activities.
cards.quote: Only then can you ask whether the foci themselves, rather than protein X alone, are needed.
